bites.title: Reading code top-down
bites.body:
Do not read code like a novel, from the first line to the last. Read it like a map: get the overall layout first, then zoom in.

Start at the entry point, the function that runs first. This is often called main, or sits under the line if __name__ == "__main__". Note which functions it calls, and in what order. That sequence is the story of the program.

Then open each function and read only its name, its inputs and what it returns. Skip the middle for now.

After five minutes you know what the program does and who is in charge of each part. Only then dive into the details that matter.
bites.sourceNote: Reading practice for generated Python · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Where should you start when reading an unfamiliar program?

choices.text: At the last line, reading upwards
At the longest function
At the list of imports only
At the entry point, to see which functions are called and in what order

questions.explanation: The entry point shows the overall flow, which gives every other part its context.

bites.title: Tracing inputs and outputs
bites.body:
Tracing means pretending to be the computer. Pick a tiny input and walk through the code one line at a time, writing down what each name holds as you go.

Take a function that averages a list. Feed it [2, 4] by hand: the total becomes 6, the count is 2, the result is 3. Good.

Now try an awkward input: an empty list. The total is 0, the count is 0, and dividing by zero crashes. You have found a bug without running anything.

Generated code is usually right for the ordinary case and wrong at the edges. Empty, zero, missing and very large inputs are where to look.
bites.sourceNote: Manual tracing as a reading technique · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Which input is most likely to reveal a hidden bug in generated code?

choices.text: A typical, ordinary input
An edge case such as an empty list
The same input the assistant used in its example
No input at all, without running anything

questions.explanation: Generated code tends to handle the normal case and fail on empty, zero or missing values.

bites.title: Spotting red flags in generated code
bites.body:
A red flag is not proof of a bug. It is a reason to slow down and read that part twice, the way a mechanic listens for a noise that should not be there.

Assistants write code that looks finished. It is tidy, commented and confident, and that polish says nothing about whether it is correct.

Useful habits: be suspicious of anything that seems too convenient, such as a library function that does exactly what you asked for. Check that comments match what the code really does. Notice what is missing, not just what is there: what happens if the file is absent, the list is empty, or the network is down?
bites.sourceNote: Review habits for AI-generated Python · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Generated code is neatly formatted and well commented. What does that tell you about its correctness?

choices.text: It is almost certainly correct
It has definitely been tested
Nothing: polish and correctness are separate things
It was written by a person

questions.explanation: Assistants always produce tidy-looking code. Whether it works can only be established by reading and testing.

bites.title: Red flags: hard-coded secrets, no error handling, invented library functions
bites.body:
Three specific warning signs are worth memorising.

Hard-coded secrets: an API key or password typed straight into the code, such as api_key = "sk-...". It should be read from an environment variable.

No error handling: network calls and file reads with nothing around them, as though nothing could fail. In real use, something always does.

Invented functions: the assistant calls something that sounds right but does not exist, like a street on a hand-drawn map that was never built. This is a hallucination. You find out with an AttributeError or ImportError, or by checking the docs.

None of these takes expertise to spot. They take the habit of looking.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: An assistant's code calls a library function that does not exist. What is this called?

choices.text: A virtual environment
A rate limit
A hallucination
A docstring

questions.explanation: Models can produce plausible but invented names. Checking the library's docs or running the code exposes them.

bites.title: Ask the assistant to explain each part, then test the explanation
bites.body:
When you do not understand a piece of code, ask the assistant to walk through it line by line in plain language. It is good at this, and it is the fastest tutor available.

But treat the explanation as a claim, not a fact. A model can explain wrong code with complete confidence, describing what the code was meant to do rather than what it does.

So test it. If the explanation says "this skips empty rows", feed it an empty row and watch. A sat-nav that says "you have arrived" is worth a glance out of the window.

Explanation plus a quick experiment is how you actually learn the code, rather than just feeling reassured.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: The assistant explains that a function "ignores blank lines". What is the best next step?

choices.text: Accept it, since explanations are always accurate
Delete the function
Ask for the same explanation again in different words
Run it with a blank line and see whether that is true

questions.explanation: An explanation is a claim about behaviour. A small test confirms whether the code really behaves that way.

bites.title: Small functions are easier to review than long scripts
bites.body:
You can only hold so much in your head at once. A 15-line function with a clear name can be checked in a minute. A 300-line script where everything touches everything cannot really be checked at all.

It is the difference between proofreading one paragraph and proofreading a whole book in one sitting. Errors slip through when attention runs out.

So when you direct an assistant, ask for small pieces: "one function that loads the file, one that cleans the rows, one that writes the report". Each can be read, tested and replaced on its own.

Small pieces also make the assistant better, because it has less to keep track of at once.
bites.sourceNote: Drafted by AI, November 2026 · confidence: high

questions.prompt: Why ask an assistant for several small functions instead of one long script?

choices.text: Each piece can be read, tested and fixed on its own
Long scripts are not allowed in Python
Small functions use no memory
It guarantees the code has no bugs

questions.explanation: Small, focused units fit in your head, which makes review and testing realistic.
